Great Britain’s electricity comes mainly from wind, natural gas, nuclear, solar, biomass, hydro, storage, and imports. In 2025, wind was the largest single source, while renewables overall supplied a record 44% of generation.

Does GB electricity mix data include Northern Ireland?

Finished

No—“GB electricity mix” normally means Great Britain only: England, Scotland, and Wales. It excludes Northern Ireland. Northern Ireland is part of the UK but operates on the all-island Ireland grid, so it is generally reported separately.
assets.publishing.service.gov
+1

Why it is excluded

Great Britain’s transmission system is operated separately from Northern Ireland’s, which is integrated with the Republic of Ireland’s grid. National Grid’s operational metering data therefore does not include generation units connected in Northern Ireland, although electricity imported through the Northern Ireland–Scotland interconnector can appear in GB figures.
assets.publishing.service.gov

What the data covers
Dataset label	Coverage
GB electricity mix / Carbon Intensity API	England, Scotland, and Wales; Northern Ireland is excluded.

How is transmission-metered wind different from embedded wind?

Finished

Transmission-metered wind is wind generation directly visible to the electricity system operator through the high-voltage transmission network. Embedded wind is distribution-connected wind that is largely invisible to that system and must be estimated from models and demand effects.

+1

Grid connection	Connected directly to the transmission network, usually at high voltage.
